title: Add AsyncKeyStore API for async PostgreSQL backend (asyncpg)
description: Add an async API surface to support a Postgres backend implemented with asyncpg without forcing sync callers into event loop management.
design:
Introduce an async-first keystore API to support async PostgreSQL drivers (asyncpg).

Design sketch:
- Add AsyncKeyStore (or a parallel API surface) with equivalent operations needed for DB-backed keystore behavior.
- Keep existing KeyStore synchronous and defaulting to SQLite (backwards compatibility).
- AsyncKeyStore should accept the same path concept but use env config to select backend; for postgres it uses asyncpg.
- Provide minimal shared business logic between KeyStore and AsyncKeyStore where feasible.

Notes:
- Avoid calling asyncio.run inside library methods (breaks callers running inside event loops).
- Consider a small adapter layer so common DB operations are implemented once per backend.
acceptance_criteria:
- AsyncKeyStore exists and can be instantiated.
- AsyncKeyStore uses asyncpg when configured for Postgres.
- Basic CRUD operations are available asynchronously (initially: connect/init schema + simple sanity op).
- Existing synchronous KeyStore remains unchanged for SQLite users.
notes: Unblocked after epic rescope: Postgres support will be delivered via AsyncKeyStore (asyncpg) directly; proceeding with implementation under 82j.
close_reason: Completed: AsyncKeyStore exists, uses asyncpg, supports schema init/ensure + basic read/write; import_key + full read parity implemented; tests cover backend and parity. Closing parent to unblock dependent tasks.

title: Implement PostgreSQL backend (asyncpg) for AsyncKeyStore
description: Rescope: Provide PostgreSQL persistence support via the async API (AsyncKeyStore) using asyncpg. Keep the existing synchronous KeyStore SQLite-only to avoid event-loop bridging. The epic is now focused on: asyncpg connection + schema init + minimal keystore operations + tests, plus wiring so backend selection via env works for AsyncKeyStore.
design:
Add a PostgreSQL backend alongside the existing SQLite backend.

Key considerations:
- Abstract DB operations behind a backend interface (connect, migrations/schema init, CRUD primitives used by the library).
- Configuration: support selecting backend via env var / config file / connection string.
- SQL compatibility: adjust queries for Postgres (parameter placeholders, returning clauses, UPSERT syntax, foreign keys, etc.).
- Migrations: either maintain neutral migrations or backend-specific; ensure initial schema can be created in Postgres.
- Connection/pooling: use a robust driver (likely psycopg/psycopg2) with pooling and proper transaction handling.
- Testing: run backend contract tests against both SQLite and Postgres; add CI service container for Postgres.

Out of scope (initial epic): performance tuning, advanced pooling, multi-tenant schemas.
acceptance_criteria:
- PostgreSQL backend is available via AsyncKeyStore using asyncpg.
- Schema is created/initialized successfully on a fresh Postgres database.
- Core keystore operations needed by AsyncKeyStore work end-to-end on Postgres (initial scope: schema init + minimal read/write proof: save_key_info + list_fingerprints).
- Existing synchronous KeyStore remains SQLite-only (no event loop bridging).
- Automated tests cover the async Postgres backend behavior (schema + minimal CRUD proof).
notes: Rescoped: implement Postgres backend via asyncpg for AsyncKeyStore; do not add sync Postgres backend behind KeyStore. This unblocks async work without event loop bridging.
close_reason: Completed: AsyncPgBackend + AsyncKeyStore provide asyncpg Postgres support including schema init/ensure, import_key with full schema writes, and full Key reconstruction; integration tests cover behavior.

title: Abstract persistence layer to remove tight coupling to SQLite
description: Create an abstraction boundary around persistence so that SQLite becomes an implementation detail rather than a hard dependency. This unlocks alternate backends and simplifies testing/portability.
design:
## Goal
Decouple persistence layer from a hard dependency on SQLite so the library can support alternate backends (e.g. Postgres, in-memory, file-based) and simplify testing.

## Current problem
The codebase appears to directly couple domain logic and/or repository operations to SQLite-specific constructs (DDL, SQL dialect, connection management, migrations).

## Target architecture (proposed)
- Define a small storage interface (e.g. `Storage`/`Repository`/`Store`) that covers required operations.
- Provide a default `sqlite` adapter implementing that interface.
- Introduce dependency injection / factory to select backend (config/env).
- Keep schema/migrations behind adapter boundary.

## Non-goals
- Rewriting all queries to a new ORM (unless chosen explicitly).
- Providing multiple production backends immediately; focus on isolating SQLite first.

## Notes
- Prefer minimal surface area: add only methods the domain needs.
- Add an in-memory or test-double adapter to speed up unit tests.
acceptance_criteria:
- Domain/service code no longer imports or calls SQLite-specific APIs directly.
- A backend interface exists with clear responsibilities and minimal methods.
- SQLite implementation is one adapter behind the interface.
- Tests can run using a non-SQLite adapter (in-memory or fake) OR SQLite can be swapped via configuration.
- Public API and CLI (if any) continue to work with SQLite backend by default.
- Clear documentation explaining how to add/choose a backend.

title: Audit current SQLite touchpoints and persistence responsibilities
description: Inventory all direct SQLite usage and classify persistence responsibilities to inform the minimal backend interface.
acceptance_criteria:
- Identify every module/function that imports SQLite directly (or uses sqlite-specific query/migration code).
- Document each dependency: why it exists, which operations it supports, and the owning layer (domain/service/infra).
- Output a short report in the issue notes (or link to a doc) listing touchpoints and suggested interface methods.
notes:
## Deeper audit: schema + method→table mapping

### SQLite schema (`johnnycanencrypt/utils.py::createdb`)
Tables:
- `keys`: stores primary key material
  - cols: `id`, `keyvalue` (BLOB), `fingerprint`, `keyid`, `expiration`, `creation`, `keytype` (int), `can_primary_sign` (int), `oncard` (text), `primary_on_card` (text)
- `subkeys`: subkey index per key
  - cols: `id`, `key_id` (FK→keys.id), `fingerprint`, `keyid`, `expiration`, `creation`, `keytype` (text), `revoked` (int)
- `uidvalues`: UID “value” strings per key
  - cols: `id`, `value`, `revoked` (int), `key_id` (FK)
- `uidcerts`: certifications per uid value
  - cols: `id`, `ctype`, `creation`, `key_id` (FK), `value_id` (FK→uidvalues.id)
- `uidcertlist`: certification details (datatype/value tuples)
  - cols: `id`, `value`, `datatype`, `key_id` (FK), `value_id` (FK), `cert_id` (FK→uidcerts.id)
- `uidemails`, `uidnames`, `uiduris`: denormalized UID lookup tables
  - cols: `id`, `value`, `key_id` (FK), `value_id` (FK)
- `dbupgrade`: single-row schema versioning (`upgradedate` TEXT)

### Migration / db lifecycle (SQLite-specific)
- `KeyStore.__init__`:
  - Creates DB file `jce.db` if missing
  - `executescript(createdb)`
  - Inserts into `dbupgrade (upgradedate)`
  - Calls `upgrade_if_required()` otherwise
- `KeyStore._upgrade_if_required`:
  - Reads `dbupgrade`
  - If missing/old: copies all rows from `keys`, builds new DB `jce_upgrade.db`, re-inserts all keys using `_save_key_info_to_db`, then patches `oncard` / `primary_on_card`.

### Method → SQL responsibilities (current)

#### Key mutation / upsert
- `_save_key_info_to_db(...)`
  - Reads: `keys` by fingerprint
  - Writes:
    - insert/update `keys`
    - insert `subkeys`
    - delete+reinsert `uidvalues`, `uidcerts`, `uidcertlist`, `uidemails`, `uidnames`, `uiduris`
  - Also contains domain merge behavior for duplicate public keys (calls `merge_keys`)

- `update_password(key, ...)`
  - Writes: `keys.keyvalue` by `keys.fingerprint`

- `update_expiry_in_subkeys(key, subkeys, ...)`
  - Writes:
    - `keys.keyvalue` by fingerprint
    - `subkeys.expiration` by `subkeys.fingerprint`

- `update_expiry_in_primary(key, ...)`
  - Writes: `keys.expiration` by fingerprint

- `add_userid(key, userid, ...)`
  - Writes:
    - `keys.keyvalue`
    - reads `keys.id` by fingerprint
    - inserts into `uidvalues` (+ corresponding `uidemails`/`uidnames`/`uiduris`)

- `revoke_userid(key, userid, ...)`
  - Writes:
    - `keys.keyvalue`
    - reads `uidvalues.id` by (key fingerprint + userid value)
    - updates `uidvalues.revoked`

- `delete_key(key|fingerprint)`
  - Reads `keys.id` by fingerprint
  - Deletes from:
    - `keys` (and then manually deletes from `subkeys`, `uidvalues`, `uidcerts`, `uidcertlist`, `uidemails`, `uidnames`, `uiduris`)
  - Note: schema already has FKs with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, but code still issues explicit deletes.

#### Key reads / queries
- `_internal_get_key(fingerprint|key_id|allkeys)`
  - Reads: `keys`
  - Delegates to `_internal_build_key_list` for joins.

- `_internal_build_key_list(rows, cursor)`
  - Reads per key:
    - `uidvalues` by `key_id`
    - `uidemails`/`uidnames`/`uiduris` by `value_id`
    - `uidcerts` by (`key_id`, `value_id`)
    - `uidcertlist` by `cert_id`
    - `subkeys` by `key_id`
  - Performs mapping into in-memory `Key` objects.

- `details()`
  - Reads: `keys (id, fingerprint, keytype)`

- `get_keys_by_keyid(keyid)`
  - Reads:
    - `keys` by `keyid`
    - `subkeys` by `keyid`
    - then `keys` by each resulting `id`

- `get_keys(qvalue, qtype)`
  - Reads from one of the denormalized tables:
    - `uidvalues` OR `uidemails` OR `uidnames` OR `uiduris`
  - Then reads full key via `_internal_get_key(key_id=...)`.

#### Smartcard linkage
- `sync_smartcard()`
  - Reads:
    - `subkeys` by fingerprint IN (sig, enc, auth) to find owning primary key id
    - `keys` by fingerprint IN (sig, enc, auth) to find if primary itself is on card
  - Writes:
    - `keys.oncard` by `keys.id`
    - `keys.primary_on_card` by `keys.id`

### Test coupling
- `tests/test_keystore.py` imports `sqlite3` directly and inspects tables (`subkeys`, `dbupgrade`).
- DB file fixtures: `tests/files/store/jce.db`, `tests/files/store/oldjce.db`.

### Implications for the persistence abstraction
- "Schema/migrations" are currently part of public `KeyStore` construction; these should move to an adapter (e.g. `SqliteBackend.migrate()` / `ensure_schema()`).
- The adapter likely needs:
  - key upsert with full replace semantics for uid/subkey/cert tables
  - read methods that return fully-hydrated `Key` models or a backend-neutral record set.

### Next
If desired, I can draft the proposed interface as a Python `Protocol` based on the above responsibilities (with async-friendly option), then add a task breakdown for moving each method onto that interface.

title: Define backend-agnostic persistence interface (minimal surface area)
description: Introduce a storage/repository interface based on the audit; keep it small and domain-focused to avoid leaking SQL concerns.
acceptance_criteria:
- Create a small backend interface (e.g. `Store`/`Repository`) capturing only required operations.
- Interface is backend-agnostic (no SQLite types leak out).
- Interface includes transaction boundaries where necessary.
- Add docstrings/comments clarifying semantics and error behavior.
notes:
## Proposed persistence interface (draft)

Given the current architecture, the simplest abstraction boundary is to extract all SQLite interaction out of `KeyStore` into a backend object that provides:

- **Schema lifecycle / migration** (currently in `KeyStore.__init__` + `_upgrade_if_required`)
- **Key CRUD/upsert** (currently `_save_key_info_to_db`, `delete_key`, `update_password`)
- **Specialized updates** (expirations, uid add/revoke, smartcard fields)
- **Query methods** (fetch by fingerprint/id, list keys, find by uid value, find by keyid)

### Design choice: return models vs raw records
Two workable options:

1) **Backend returns backend-neutral records** (dataclasses) and `KeyStore` performs mapping/assembly.
   - Pros: backend logic simpler, domain owns its model.
   - Cons: current mapping is deeply SQL-join driven; would require designing query shapes.

2) **Backend returns fully built `Key` models** (or a `KeyRecord` that matches `Key` ctor inputs).
   - Pros: minimal refactor because `_internal_build_key_list` can live inside SQLite adapter.
   - Cons: backend depends on domain model; less pure layering.

Given current constraints, (2) is the lowest-risk first step; later can refactor toward (1).

### Suggested `Protocol` interface (sync)
(Names intentionally generic; SQLite is just one implementation.)

````python
from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Protocol, Iterable, Optional, List, Union

from . import Key

KeyId = int

class KeyStoreBackend(Protocol):
    # --- lifecycle ---
    def ensure_schema(self, *, store_dir: Path) -> Path:
        """Ensure storage is initialized/migrated. Returns db path (or backend identifier)."""

    # --- primary read APIs ---
    def get_key(self, fingerprint: str) -> Key: ...
    def get_keys(self, *, allkeys: bool = False) -> List[Key]: ...
    def get_key_by_db_id(self, key_id: KeyId) -> Key: ...

    # --- lookup APIs ---
    def get_keys_by_keyid(self, keyid: str) -> List[Key]: ...
    def find_keys_by_uid(self, *, qtype: str, qvalue: str) -> List[Key]: ...

    # --- writes / mutations ---
    def upsert_parsed_key(self, cert: bytes, *, allow_public_merge: bool = True) -> None:
        """Insert/update key, including subkeys/uids/certs, based on parsing cert bytes."""

    def update_key_bytes(self, *, fingerprint: str, keyvalue: bytes) -> None: ...
    def update_key_expiration(self, *, fingerprint: str, expiration: Optional[float]) -> None: ...
    def update_subkey_expiration(self, *, subkey_fingerprint: str, expiration: Optional[float]) -> None: ...

    def add_uid_value(self, *, fingerprint: str, uid_value: str, revoked: bool = False) -> None:
        """Optional helper; might be unnecessary if `upsert_parsed_key` always fully replaces uids."""

    def revoke_uid_value(self, *, fingerprint: str, uid_value: str) -> None: ...

    def delete_key(self, fingerprint: str) -> None: ...

    # --- smartcard linkage ---
    def set_oncard_by_subkeys(self, *, sig_f: str, enc_f: str, auth_f: str, serial: str) -> Optional[str]:
        """Find owning primary key by subkey fingerprints, set oncard field, return primary fingerprint."""

    def set_primary_on_card(self, *, fingerprint: str, serial: str) -> None: ...
````

### Notes on mapping existing code to interface
- `KeyStore.__init__` becomes: `self.dbpath = backend.ensure_schema(store_dir=fullpath)`
- `_save_key_info_to_db` collapses into `backend.upsert_parsed_key(cert)` (SQLite adapter can reuse existing insert logic).
- `_internal_get_key` + `_internal_build_key_list` become backend responsibility (SQLite adapter keeps SQL).
- `get_keys()` / `get_keys_by_keyid()` become backend calls.
- Smartcard `sync_smartcard()` becomes: parse card fingerprints in service layer, then call `backend.set_oncard_by_subkeys(...)` and/or `backend.set_primary_on_card(...)`.

### Async considerations (future)
There are `.pyc` artifacts suggesting async modules existed; if async is required, define a parallel `AsyncKeyStoreBackend` with `async def` methods mirroring the above.

### Recommendation
Implement the backend interface first with a `SqliteKeyStoreBackend` that is largely a mechanical move of the existing sqlite code out of `KeyStore`.

Next: implement a `Null/InMemoryBackend` for unit tests (minimal subset), then gradually migrate tests away from direct `sqlite3` access.

smartcardtests/smartcards.py: error: Duplicate module named "smartcards" (also at "./sm2/smartcards.py")
smartcardtests/smartcards.py: note: See https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html#mapping-file-paths-to-modules for more info
